She was initially admitted in pediatric ward with a diagnosis of croup and treated with oxygen and steroids. Lack of symptomatic improvement on the following day raised suspicion of FB.
Then, the patient was referred to Patan Academy of Health Sciences (PAHS) with an uncuffed tracheostomy tube.

At PAHS, rigid bronchoscopy was attempted; however, the FB was not visualised upon advancing the bronchoscope into the trachea. Flexible bronchoscopy through the tracheostomy tube also failed to locate the FB up to the primary bronchus. Due to the child’s unstable condition, the tracheostomy tube was left in place, and the procedure was abandoned. A post-operative CT scan revealed the FB had migrated to the left main bronchus (Figure 2).

An initial rigid bronchoscopy was performed without removing the tracheostomy tube, as the foreign body (FB) was located above its level. During attempted extraction, the FB became dislodged. Subsequent flexible bronchoscopy through the tracheostomy tube failed to visualize the FB up to the primary bronchi, and the procedure was aborted due to hemodynamic instability. A second rigid bronchoscopy was performed 8 to 10 hours later following removal of the tracheostomy tube.

summary.text: A 3-year-old female presented with two days of cough and difficulty in breathing, was initially treated with nebulization at a local health center, then admitted to a pediatric ward as croup and given oxygen and steroids. Lack of improvement on the following day and a parental history of sudden coughing while eating raised suspicion of a foreign body, and X-ray soft tissue neck showed a foreign body in the subglottic airway.

The family was counseled about rigid bronchoscopy and tracheostomy for safe transfer, tracheostomy was performed, and an X-ray after tracheostomy still showed the subglottic foreign body. She was referred to PAHS with an uncuffed tracheostomy tube, where a first rigid bronchoscopy was attempted (the article gives two differing accounts of it), a flexible bronchoscopy failed to locate the foreign body and the procedure was abandoned and a post-operative CT scan showed the foreign body in the left main bronchus.

A second rigid bronchoscopy 8 to 10 hours later, with the tracheostomy tube removed and reinserted, extracted a 2.5*2 cm bone chip with telescope-mounted forceps. Because of the prolonged surgery and mucosal inflammation and tears she was kept in high care with the tracheostomy tube in place, and intravenous antibiotics and steroids were prescribed. She was decannulated on the fourth postoperative day, tolerated this and was discharged the same day.

ambiguities.issue: The first rigid bronchoscopy is described incompatibly: the PAHS paragraph (b00005) says the FB was not visualised upon advancing the bronchoscope into the trachea, while the next paragraph (b00006) says the FB was located above the tube level and became dislodged during attempted extraction; the abstract says it migrated during the first attempt. The procedure is kept once as performed (p1-f022) and the two findings are quarantined as source_conflict facts.

During attempted extraction, the FB became dislodged.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not choose one account, reconcile them, or infer a second separate first-stage attempt.

ambiguities.issue: The cause of the FB migration is the authors’ hypothesis (manipulation, uncuffed tube, thin FB), not a documented finding.

evidence.quote: the FB migrated into the left main bronchus, likely due to manipulation and the use of an uncuffed tracheostomy tube
It is hypothesized that during the initial rigid bronchoscopy, the FB may have been pushed further down the airway and subsequently migrated to the bronchus.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not record manipulation or the uncuffed tube as an established cause.

ambiguities.issue: The discussion says rigid bronchoscopy was tried 'even after identification of FB location after imaging (CT scan)', which could place a CT before the first rigid attempt or refer to the second rigid bronchoscopy; the case text calls the CT post-operative, after the abandoned first procedure. The discussion also calls the FB a suspected bone while the case reports a retrieved bone chip.

evidence.quote: In our case we initially tried with rigid bronchoscope even after identification of FB location after imaging (CT scan).
A post-operative CT scan revealed the FB had migrated to the left main bronchus (Figure 2).

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not place a CT scan before the first bronchoscopy; the case text dates the CT after the attempt.

ambiguities.issue: The route is stated as "Intravenous antibiotics and steroids"; the route is recorded for antibiotics only and not borrowed for steroids.
